entries.0ce2a7ebf3bfa172ffb818ba8eb1f388122b6766: <div sID="gen2419" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="Lev.14" sID="Lev.14"/> <div eID="gen2419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2420" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen2421" type="x-p"/> The former chapter directed the priests how to convict a leper of ceremonial uncleanness. No prescriptions are given for his cure; but, when God had cured him, the priests are in this chapter directed how to cleanse him. The remedy here is only adapted to the ceremonial part of his disease; but the authority Christ gave to his ministers was to cure the lepers, and so to cleanse them. We have here, I. The solemn declaration of the leper's being clean, with the significant ceremony attending it, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.1-Lev.14.9">ver. 1-9</reference>. II. The sacrifices which he was to offer to God eight days after, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.10-Lev.14.32">ver. 10-32</reference>. III. The management of a house in which appeared signs of a leprosy, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.33-Lev.14.53">ver. 33-53</reference>. And the conclusion and summary of this whole matter, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.54-Lev.14.57">ver. 54</reference>, &c.
entries.cc7135e91ec1e5d12380266d3cc33bbd6937698b: <div eID="gen2421" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen2420" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Law Concerning Leprosy. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1490.)</title> <div sID="gen2422" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spake unto Moses, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> This shall be the law of the leper in the day of his cleansing: He shall be brought unto the priest: <hi type="super">3</hi> And the priest shall go forth out of the camp; and the priest shall look, and, behold, <hi type="italic">if</hi> the plague of leprosy be healed in the leper; <hi type="super">4</hi> Then shall the priest command to take for him that is to be cleansed two birds alive <hi type="italic">and</hi> clean, and cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop: <hi type="super">5</hi> And the priest shall command that one of the birds be killed in an earthen vessel over running water: <hi type="super">6</hi> As for the living bird, he shall take it, and the cedar wood, and the scarlet, and the hyssop, and shall dip them and the living bird in the blood of the bird <hi type="italic">that was</hi> killed over the running water: <hi type="super">7</hi> And he shall sprinkle upon him that is to be cleansed from the leprosy seven times, and shall pronounce him clean, and shall let the living bird loose into the open field. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he that is to be cleansed shall wash his clothes, and shave off all his hair, and wash himself in water, that he may be clean: and after that he shall come into the camp, and shall tarry abroad out of his tent seven days. <hi type="super">9</hi> But it shall be on the seventh day, that he shall shave all his hair off his head and his beard and his eyebrows, even all his hair he shall shave off: and he shall wash his clothes, also he shall wash his flesh in water, and he shall be clean. <div eID="gen2422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2423" type="x-p"/> Here, I. It is supposed that the plague of the leprosy was not an incurable disease. Uzziah's indeed continued to the day of his death, and Gehazi's was entailed upon his seed; but Miriam's lasted only seven days: we may suppose that it often wore off in process of time. Though God contend long, he will <hi type="italic">not contend for ever.</hi> <div eID="gen2423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2424" type="x-p"/> II. The judgment of the cure, as well as that of the disease, was referred to the priest. He must go out of the camp to the leper, to see whether his leprosy was healed, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.3">v. 3</reference>. And we may suppose the priest did not contract any ceremonial uncleanness by coming near the leper, as another person would. It was in mercy to the poor lepers that the priests particularly had orders to attend them, for <hi type="italic">the priests' lips should keep knowledge;</hi> and those in affliction have need to be instructed both how to bear their afflictions and how to reap benefit by them, have need of the word, in concurrence with the rod, to bring them to repentance; therefore it is well for those that are sick if they have these messengers of the Lord of hosts with them, these interpreters, to <hi type="italic">show unto them God's uprightness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.33.23">Job xxxiii. 23</reference>. When the leper was shut out, and could not go to the priests, it was well that the priests might come to him. <hi type="italic">Is any sick? Let him send for the elders,</hi> the ministers, <reference osisRef="Jas.5.14">Jam. v. 14</reference>. If we apply it to the spiritual leprosy of sin, it intimates that when we withdraw from those who walk disorderly, that they may be ashamed, we must not count them as enemies, but admonish them as brethren, <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.15">2 Thess. iii. 15</reference>. And also that when God by his grace has brought those to repentance who were shut out of communion for scandal, they ought with tenderness, and joy, and sincere affection, to be received in again. Thus Paul orders concerning the excommunicated Corinthian that when he had given evidences of his repentance they should forgive him, and comfort him, and <hi type="italic">confirm their love towards him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7-2Cor.2.8">2 Cor. ii. 7, 8</reference>. And ministers are entrusted by our Master with the declarative power of loosing as well as binding: both must be done with great caution and deliberation, impartially and without respect of persons, with earnest prayer to God for directions, and a sincere regard to the edification of the body of Christ, due care being always taken that sinners may not be encouraged by an excess of lenity, nor penitents discouraged by an excess of severity. Wisdom and sincerity are profitable to direct in this case. <div eID="gen2424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2425" type="x-p"/> III. If it was found that the leprosy was healed, the priest must declare it with a particular solemnity. The leper or his friends were to get ready two birds caught for this purpose (any sort of wild birds that were clean), and cedar-wood, and scarlet, and hyssop; for all these were to be used in the ceremony. 1. A preparation was to be made of blood and water, with which the leper must be sprinkled. One of the birds (and the Jews say, if there was any difference, it must be the larger and better of the two) was to be killed over an earthen cup of spring water, so that the blood of the bird might discolour the water. This (as some other types) had its accomplishment in the death of Christ, when out of his pierced side there came water and blood, <reference osisRef="John.19.34">John xix. 34</reference>. Thus Christ comes into the soul for its cure and cleansing, <hi type="italic">not by water only, but by water and blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.5.6">1 John v. 6</reference>. 2. The living bird, with a little scarlet wool, and a bunch of hyssop, must be fastened to a cedar stick, dipped in the water and blood, which must be so sprinkled upon him that was to be cleansed, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.6-Lev.14.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. The cedar-wood signified the restoring of the leper to his strength and soundness, for that is a sort of wood not apt to putrefy. The scarlet wool signified his recovering a florid colour again, for the leprosy made him white as snow. And the hyssop intimated the removing of the disagreeable scent which commonly attended the leprosy. The cedar the stateliest plant, and hyssop the meanest, are here used together in this service (see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.33">1 Kings iv. 33</reference>); for those of the lowest rank in the church may be of use in their place, as well as those that are most eminent, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.2">1 Cor. xii. 2</reference>. Some make the slain bird to typify Christ <hi type="italic">dying for our sins,</hi> and the living bird Christ <hi type="italic">rising again for our justification.</hi> The dipping of the living bird in the blood of the slain bird intimated that the merit of Christ's death was that which made his resurrection effectual for our justification. He took his blood with him into the holy place, and there appeared a lamb as it had been slain. The cedar, scarlet wool, and hyssop, must all be dipped in the blood; for the word and ordinances, and all the operations of the Spirit, receive their efficacy for our cleansing from the blood of Christ. The leper must be sprinkled <hi type="italic">seven times,</hi> to signify a complete purification, in allusion to which David prays, <hi type="italic">Wash me thoroughly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.51.2">Ps. li. 2</reference>. Naaman was directed to wash <hi type="italic">seven times,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.5.10">2 Kings v. 10</reference>. 3. The living bird was then to be let loose in the open field, to signify that the leper, being cleansed, was now no longer under restraint and confinement, but might take his liberty to go where he pleased. But this being signified by the flight of a bird towards heaven was an intimation to him henceforward to seek the things that are above, and not to spend this new life to which God had restored him merely in the pursuit of earthly things. This typified that glorious liberty of the children of God to which those are advanced who through grace are sprinkled from an evil conscience. Those whose souls before <hi type="italic">bowed down to the dust</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.44.25">Ps. xliv. 25</reference>), in grief and fear, now fly in the open firmament of heaven, and soar upwards upon the wings of faith and hope, and holy love and joy. 4. The priest must, upon this, pronounce him clean. It was requisite that this should be done with solemnity, that the leper might himself be the more affected with the mercy of God to him in his recovery, and that others might be satisfied to converse with him. Christ is our priest, to whom the Father has committed all judgment, and particularly the judgment of the leprosy. By his definitive sentence impenitent sinners will have their everlasting portion assigned them with the unclean (<reference osisRef="Job.36.14">Job xxxvi. 14</reference>), out of the holy city; and all that by his grace are cured and cleansed shall be received into the camp of the saints, into which no unclean thing shall enter. Those are clean indeed whom Christ pronounces so, and they need not regard what men say of them. But, though Christ was the <hi type="italic">end of this law for righteousness,</hi> yet being in the days of his flesh <hi type="italic">made under the law,</hi> which as yet stood unrepealed, he ordered those lepers whom he had cured miraculously to go and <hi type="italic">show themselves to the priest,</hi> and <hi type="italic">offer for their cleansing according to the law,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.8.4">Matt. viii. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.17.14">Luke xvii. 14</reference>. The type must be kept up till it was answered by its antitype. 5. When the leper was pronounced clean, he must wash his body and his clothes, and shave <hi type="italic">off all his hair</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lev.14.8">v. 8</reference>), must still tarry seven days out of the camp, and on the seventh day must do it again, <reference osisRef="Lev.14.9">v. 9</reference>. The priest having pronounced him clean from the disease, he must make himself as clean as ever he could from all the remains of it, and from all other defilements, and he must take time to do this. Thus those who have the comfort of the remission of their sins, by the sprinkling of the blood of Christ upon their consciences, must with the utmost care and caution <hi type="italic">cleanse themselves from all filthiness both of flesh and spirit,</hi> and thoroughly <hi type="italic">purge themselves from their old sins;</hi> for <hi type="italic">every one that hath this hope in him will</hi> be concerned to <hi type="italic">purify himself.</hi>
